teaser: The title promises a beloved woman. The canvas delivers petals, coils and spark plugs.
review_notes:
IMAGE: this is a gallery photograph taken at an angle; it shows the frame at the bottom and appears cropped at the top and sides (the canvas is about 250 x 199 cm, less elongated than this image). Coordinates refer to the photo as it is.
Date: MoMA gives 1914, possibly begun 1913.
Stacia Napierkowska met on the 1913 crossing to New York; her arrest in New York for an 'indecent' dance during that tour: fairly sure, please check.
Origin of the name 'Udnie' is unknown; the theories given (Jean d'Udine, an anagram of 'nudie', 'Undine') are presented as guesses.
'More than a hundred cars' is the commonly repeated figure (often 127).
The inscription in the lower left corner is faint in this photo; the find block uses a wide marker.

lesson.text: Read the title first: I See Again in Memory My Dear Udnie. It sounds like the opening of a love letter. Now search the picture for her. There is no face, no figure, no room. There are pale swollen shapes, ribbed red collars, gray shells and something like a light bulb. The words are tender and the forms are closer to engine parts.

There was a real woman behind the name. In January 1913 Francis Picabia sailed to New York for the Armory Show, the exhibition that introduced modern art to America. On the ship he watched a dancer rehearse: Stacia Napierkowska, a star of the Paris stage and of early cinema. He never forgot it.

Napierkowska's act was daring for 1913. During that same American tour, New York police arrested her on the grounds that her dance was indecent. The scandal only added to her fame, and probably to Picabia's fascination.

Back in Paris, Picabia painted not the dancer but the memory of the dancer, a year later and an ocean away. A memory is not a photograph. It is heat, rhythm, fragments, a color. Nobody knows for sure where “Udnie” comes from. It may scramble a word or hide a name, and Picabia enjoyed never explaining.

The canvas is huge, about 2.5 meters high (over 8 feet), so these shapes are larger than your own body. Cold grays and blacks circle the outside. In the middle, a warm column of cream, pink, orange and red seems to climb and unfold. Three of its parts are worth meeting up close.

lesson.title: Flesh or machine?
lesson.text: Each form can be read two ways at once. That double reading is the subject.

spots.title: The cream form
spots.text: Four pale lobes with ochre seams, soft as petals or fingers. It swells like something alive, yet its edges are as clean as a pressed metal part.

spots.title: The ribbed collar
spots.text: A stack of red rings clamps the pale form at its base, like the thread of a screw or a rubber hose fitting. A second one sits just below, to the right.

spots.title: The flame
spots.text: A yellow tongue with a dark split inside a black cup, set on a row of beads. A candle, a burner or a spark plug. It is the hottest point in the picture.

lesson.text: Petals, limbs, valves, plugs: the forms slide between a body and a machine and never settle. Picabia is painting desire, and he chooses the vocabulary of plumbing and electricity to do it. Abstract art in 1914 was supposed to be pure and spiritual. His is cheerfully physical.

Machines were Picabia's other passion. Born rich, the son of a Cuban-Spanish diplomat and a French mother, he bought fast automobiles the way other men bought hats. Friends counted more than a hundred over his lifetime.

One element of the painting is not a shape at all. Picabia worried so little about the purity of abstraction that he added a caption, by hand, on the canvas itself. In this photograph it is dim and partly cut off, close to the frame.
The title is written on the painting in small capital letters. Which corner?

spots.title: The inscription
spots.text: Lower left, just above the frame: the French words “...en souvenir ma chère Udnie”, in thin dark capitals. On the opposite side, at lower right, you can make out the signature, Picabia.

lesson.text: Those few words change how the whole thing works. Without them you would see a handsome arrangement of forms. With them, you start hunting for a woman, a dance, a ship, and the hunt never ends. Picabia had found that a title can be a material of the picture, like paint.
The painting does not show a memory, it behaves like one: warm, fragmentary, impossible to pin down. And it lets words do part of the painting's job.

A year later, in New York, Picabia went one step further and drew his friends as actual machines: a camera, a spark plug, a lamp, each with a mocking caption. Out of that mix of mechanics, sex and jokes came Dada, the movement that set out to wreck serious art. This large canvas at the Museum of Modern Art shows that turn starting.

quiz.question: Who inspired the painting?
options: A dancer Picabia saw on a ship to New York
A fictional nymph from a poem
quiz.explanation: He watched Stacia Napierkowska rehearse during the 1913 crossing.

quiz.question: How do the central forms differ from the ones around them?
options: They are gray, the outside is red
They are warm in color, the outside is gray and black
quiz.explanation: A warm column of cream, pink and red sits inside cold grays.

quiz.question: What did Picabia write on the canvas?
quiz.explanation: The title is lettered in the lower left corner.

quiz.question: What two things do the shapes seem to be at once?
quiz.explanation: They hover between living forms and mechanical fittings.

quiz.question: Which movement grew out of Picabia's mix of machines and jokes?
quiz.explanation: His machine portraits of 1915 fed directly into Dada.

facts.text: The painting contains a recognizable portrait of a dancer.
facts.explanation: There is no figure at all, only abstract forms.

facts.text: Picabia painted it from memory, about a year after the voyage.
facts.explanation: The crossing was in 1913 and the canvas dates from 1914.

facts.text: The meaning of the name “Udnie” is well documented.
facts.explanation: Its origin is unknown and Picabia never explained it.
